I would rather be honest: the depth that rigorous training opens up is irreplaceable, and pretending otherwise does no one any favors.
How does the decline in piano instruction in homes affect the general public's musical literacy?

The disappearance of the piano from the home is one of the most consequential cultural losses of the past century, and its effects on musical literacy are profound and largely unacknowledged. The piano was not merely an instrument — it was a complete musical education sitting in your living room. Through it, a person encountered harmony vertically and melody horizontally. They learned to coordinate independent voices, to feel the architecture of a phrase, to understand why a diminished seventh chord creates tension and a resolution satisfies. This was embodied knowledge, not abstract theory.

When families gathered around a piano, they weren't just entertaining themselves — they were developing ears capable of hearing music from the inside. A person who has struggled through even a simple Bach invention understands counterpoint in a way that no amount of passive listening can replicate. They grasp that music has logic, that it argues and develops, that form is not decoration but meaning.

What we've lost is not just a skill but a perceptual capacity. The general public today hears music as surface — as mood, as rhythm, as vibe. And while those are real dimensions of musical experience, they represent only the outermost layer. Without the foundational literacy that piano study provided, most listeners simply cannot perceive the harmonic motion, the voice-leading, the structural drama that distinguishes genuinely great music from the merely pleasant. We've traded a culture of musical participants for one of musical consumers, and the impoverishment runs deeper than most people realize.
Is it important for listeners, not just performers, to understand music theory?

You can walk through the Alhambra and find it beautiful without understanding Islamic geometric principles, but your experience of it will be fundamentally shallower. The same holds for music. When you hear the recapitulation in a Beethoven sonata without understanding what a recapitulation *does* — how it resolves the tonal drama of the exposition and development — you're receiving perhaps thirty percent of what the composer intended. You're hearing the surface while the architecture passes you by. I don't mean that every listener needs to sit down with a Schenkerian graph. But the basic grammar of music — how tension and resolution work, what modulation achieves, how rhythm creates expectation and surprise — this is not arcane specialist knowledge. It's the difference between reading a novel and having someone describe the plot to you. The great irony is that people readily accept this principle in other domains. No one objects when a wine educator explains that understanding terroir and fermentation deepens appreciation. No one calls it gatekeeping when a film professor teaches shot composition. Yet suggest that understanding sonata form might enhance one's experience of Schubert, and suddenly you're accused of elitism. The truth is that composers like Bach, Bartók, and Coltrane were thinking in theoretical terms when they created their works. Their music *encodes* theoretical relationships. To refuse to meet them on those terms is not democratic humility — it's a kind of incuriosity that ultimately shortchanges the listener themselves. Even a modest investment in theory opens doors that remain permanently closed to the purely passive ear.
What role should masterclasses and mentorship play in developing advanced musicianship?

There is simply no substitute for the direct transmission of musical understanding from master to student. I say this not as an abstraction but from lived experience — the moments that most profoundly shaped my musicianship were not found in textbooks or practice rooms alone, but in the presence of artists who had internalized decades of interpretive wisdom and could communicate it through a single gesture, a sung phrase, a pointed question about why I chose a particular fingering or breath.

The masterclass tradition preserves something essential: an unbroken chain of musical thought connecting the present to the deepest wells of a tradition. When a student works with a mentor who studied with someone who studied with Nadia Boulanger, or who absorbed the phrasing traditions of a particular gharana, something passes between them that no recording or tutorial can replicate — an embodied understanding of style, proportion, and taste.

What concerns me about contemporary musical culture is the assumption that mentorship is optional, that one can assemble equivalent knowledge from YouTube videos and online forums. Technical information, yes. But advanced musicianship is not primarily about information — it is about judgment, about learning to hear the difference between what is correct and what is alive. A great mentor doesn't simply tell you what to do; they model a relationship to music that is rigorous, searching, and deeply personal. They challenge your assumptions, reveal your blind spots, and hold you to standards you didn't know you could reach. This kind of formation requires presence, trust, and time. It cannot be algorithmically delivered.
How does learning to play chamber music develop skills that solo practice cannot?

I'll say something that may sound provocative but that I believe deeply: a musician who has never seriously engaged with chamber music is, in a meaningful sense, an incomplete musician. The practice room develops technique, interpretive imagination, and self-discipline — all essential. But it cannot teach you to *listen* in the way that great music-making demands.

Consider what happens in a string quartet rehearsal of, say, Beethoven's Op. 132. Four musicians must negotiate the most intimate and demanding musical conversation ever conceived. Every phrase requires real-time decisions about who leads, who yields, how a crescendo is shaped collectively, where a ritardando breathes. The slow movement alone — that extraordinary "Heiliger Dankgesang" — demands a kind of spiritual unanimity that no amount of individual preparation can produce. You must hear your colleagues' intentions before they fully materialize in sound, and respond with your whole musical being.

This cultivates what I'd call *musical empathy* — the ability to subordinate ego to a larger artistic vision while still contributing one's full individuality. It develops intonation not as a fixed technical achievement but as a living, responsive practice. It teaches that a perfectly executed passage means nothing if it doesn't serve the ensemble's collective breath.

The great chamber musicians I've known — and I've been fortunate to study with several — all share a quality of listening that soloists sometimes lack: a porousness, an openness to being changed by what they hear in the moment. This is not a supplementary skill. It is, I would argue, the very essence of musicianship. Solo practice builds the instrument; chamber music teaches you what the instrument is for.
What is the value of memorizing and performing the standard repertoire for a developing musician?

There is no substitute for it — none whatsoever. When a developing musician commits a great work to memory and lives inside it through repeated performance, something happens that no amount of improvisation exercises or creative exploration can replicate. You begin to understand from the inside how a master builder constructs a musical argument. You feel the tension of a deceptive cadence in your fingers, your breath, your body. You internalize centuries of accumulated wisdom about what makes music cohere, surprise, and move. Consider what it means to truly memorize a Beethoven sonata. You are not simply storing notes; you are absorbing an entire architecture of motivic development, harmonic rhythm, and dramatic pacing. That knowledge becomes part of your musical instinct. When you later compose or improvise, you draw on a reservoir of structural understanding that is simply unavailable to someone who has never undertaken this discipline. The standard repertoire exists as a standard for good reason — these works have survived because they reward the deepest possible engagement. Each return reveals new layers. I have performed certain Bach Partitas dozens of times over decades, and I am still discovering relationships I had missed. This is the hallmark of genuine greatness in composition: inexhaustibility. Some will say this approach is narrow, that it privileges one tradition. But every serious musical tradition has its canonical works and its expectation of mastery through absorption — the ragas, the maqamat, the bebop heads. The principle is universal: you must first learn to speak the language of the masters before you can find your own voice within it. Shortcuts here produce shallow artists.
How should music critics balance personal taste with objective analysis when reviewing performances?

I'd push back on the premise slightly. The dichotomy between 'personal taste' and 'objective analysis' is less clean than it appears. A critic who has spent decades immersed in the repertoire — who has heard dozens of *Winterreise* cycles, who understands the harmonic language from the inside, who knows what the human voice can and cannot do — that critic's 'personal taste' is not arbitrary preference. It is educated perception. It is, in a meaningful sense, a refined instrument for detecting quality.

This is what separates criticism from mere opinion. When I note that a pianist's voicing in the inner parts of a Brahms intermezzo was muddy, or that a conductor's pacing obliterated the architectural proportions of a symphonic movement, I am not simply reporting a feeling. I am applying knowledge — of the score, of the tradition, of what other great interpreters have revealed in the same music. The discerning critic's taste has been shaped by thousands of hours of deep listening and study. To dismiss that as mere subjectivity is to suggest that a master sommelier's palate is no more reliable than a casual drinker's.

Of course, genuine humility is essential. One must remain open to interpretive choices that challenge expectations — some of the greatest performances in history defied convention. But openness to surprise is not the same as abandoning standards. The critic's duty is to serve the art: to articulate why a performance succeeded or failed in realizing the music's potential, drawing on the fullest possible understanding of what that potential is. Anything less is not criticism — it is consumer reporting.
What makes a piece of music intellectually rewarding versus merely emotionally stimulating?

I want to push back on the word 'merely' in this question — not because emotional stimulation doesn't matter, but because the distinction is real and worth defending. A piece of music becomes intellectually rewarding when it demands something of the listener: sustained attention, memory, the ability to track simultaneous processes, and a willingness to sit with ambiguity before resolution arrives. Consider the first movement of Beethoven's Op. 131 quartet — that slow fugue doesn't grab you by the collar. It asks you to follow four independent voices weaving through remote keys, and the reward comes from perceiving how those voices relate, diverge, and converge. That is a fundamentally different experience from being swept up by a well-placed key change in a pop ballad. Both involve feeling, but one engages the full architecture of musical cognition. The intellectually rewarding piece tends to have what I'd call 'depth of surface' — every re-listening reveals new relationships, new details, new questions. A Bartók string quartet, a Coltrane solo over 'Giant Steps,' a Ravi Shankar alap — these are experiences that grow richer as your knowledge deepens. Emotional stimulation, by contrast, often operates through well-worn formulas: predictable harmonic patterns, familiar timbral cues, lyrics that direct your feelings for you. I don't dismiss this — it has its place. But the discerning listener recognizes that music capable of engaging both the intellect and the emotions simultaneously represents a higher order of artistic achievement. The greatest works don't ask you to choose between thinking and feeling; they make thinking a form of feeling.
Is there a crisis in contemporary classical music, and if so, what is its cause?

There is indeed a crisis, though its nature is frequently misdiagnosed. The problem is not that audiences have shrunk—audiences for demanding art have always been modest. The deeper crisis is one of nerve and continuity within the tradition itself. For much of the twentieth century, the academy split into warring factions: the serialists pursued a rigorous but often hermetic path, while their opponents sometimes retreated into pastiche or surrendered to the marketplace. What was lost in this fracture was the living chain of craft—the sense that a composer must internalize the achievements of the past before earning the right to extend them. Bach studied Buxtehude; Beethoven absorbed Haydn; Bartók transformed folk materials through a technique forged from deep study of Bach and Debussy. Today, too many young composers emerge from conservatories having barely engaged with counterpoint or orchestration at the level their predecessors took for granted. Simultaneously, institutions have capitulated to a misguided accessibility agenda—programming crossover events, film music concerts, and 'relaxed' formats that strip the concert experience of the very concentration that makes it transformative. The discerning listener doesn't need to be coddled; they need to be challenged. And the composer doesn't need to court Spotify algorithms; they need to wrestle with the full weight of the tradition. The crisis, ultimately, is a loss of seriousness—a collective failure to insist that art music demands something extraordinary from both its creators and its audience, and that this demand is precisely what makes it irreplaceable.
How do we evaluate the cultural significance of a musical tradition that has a small audience?

The size of an audience tells us almost nothing about the significance of a musical tradition. If anything, the correlation often runs the other way. The traditions that demand the most from their practitioners and listeners — that refuse to simplify, that insist on years of apprenticeship and attentive study — will almost by definition attract smaller audiences. This is not a failure. It is a feature of depth.

Consider the North Indian dhrupad tradition, kept alive by a handful of families and a modest circle of devoted listeners. Its significance is immense — not because of audience numbers but because of the extraordinary refinement of its raga development, the sophistication of its rhythmic structures, and the centuries of accumulated wisdom embedded in its practice. Or consider the art of fugal composition after Bach: a tradition with a vanishingly small audience of practitioners, yet one that represents perhaps the highest achievement in contrapuntal thinking humanity has produced.

The discerning listener evaluates a tradition by asking: What does it demand? What does it reveal to those who meet its demands? How deep can one go before reaching its limits? A tradition with inexhaustible depth — where decades of study continue to yield new understanding — possesses a kind of significance that no popularity metric can capture.

The modern impulse to equate significance with reach is a category error born of our quantified age. A tradition's cultural significance lies in the quality of attention it cultivates, the mastery it requires, and the richness of the musical experience it makes possible for those willing to do the work.
What is the role of difficulty and effort in the listener's aesthetic experience?

I'll put this simply, from decades of lived experience: the most profound aesthetic experiences of my life have all required something of me. The first time I truly heard the architecture of a late Beethoven quartet — not just heard it, but followed its logic, felt its weight — came after months of returning to those works, score in hand, gradually learning to hear what was always there. That breakthrough was not incidental to the experience; it was the experience. There is a kind of pleasure available only on the far side of effort, a pleasure that is categorically different from the instant gratification of a catchy hook. This is not elitism — it is simply an observation about how deep engagement works. A practiced reader does not enjoy poetry less than a casual one; they enjoy it more, and differently. The same is true of the discerning listener. When you can hear the way Bach layers voices in a fugue, or follow Coltrane's harmonic substitutions in real time, or perceive the rhythmic cycles in a Carnatic performance, you are not performing some academic exercise — you are accessing a dimension of beauty that is genuinely there in the music, waiting for ears prepared to receive it. I worry that our culture increasingly treats any demand placed on the listener as an imposition rather than an invitation. But the greatest works of music are not consumer products designed for frictionless consumption. They are invitations to grow. The effort is not a barrier to the reward — it is inseparable from it.
Should art be expected to challenge and elevate its audience, or simply entertain?

If art is not expected to challenge its audience in some meaningful way, then we have abandoned the very thing that distinguishes art from mere diversion. Entertainment is abundant — it surrounds us, fills every idle moment, asks nothing, and leaves nothing behind. Art, at its best, does something fundamentally different. It reshapes how we hear, how we see, how we understand time and feeling and form. That is not a burden placed on the audience; it is a gift, though one that requires effort to unwrap.

Consider what happens when you genuinely engage with a late Beethoven quartet, or with the structural audacity of a Coltrane improvisation, or with the way Tàrrega reimagined the guitar's expressive possibilities. These experiences are not reducible to enjoyment, though enjoyment is certainly part of them. They expand the listener's inner world. They demand that you grow toward the work rather than expecting the work to shrink toward you.

I am not saying entertainment has no place — life would be grim without it. But the conflation of entertainment with art's primary purpose represents a profound diminishment. When we stop expecting art to challenge us, we stop developing the faculties needed to receive what the greatest works offer. The discerning listener knows that the most rewarding musical experiences often begin in discomfort or confusion and resolve into something far deeper than pleasure. To lower that expectation is not generosity toward the audience — it is a kind of abandonment. We owe each other more than comfort. Art, when it fulfills its highest calling, is how we prove that.
How does the critical reception of music differ between experts and the general public, and whose judgment should carry more weight?

Expertise matters, and it matters enormously. The trained listener hears more — not metaphorically, but literally. Years of study, close listening, and immersion in a tradition develop perceptual capacities that are simply unavailable to the casual listener. When a musicologist identifies the extraordinary voice-leading in a Bach chorale or a jazz critic recognizes how a pianist is reharmonizing standards in conversation with Bill Evans and Herbie Hancock simultaneously, they are perceiving real features of the music that the untrained ear passes over.

This doesn't mean the public's response is worthless — far from it. Immediate emotional impact is a genuine musical value, and sometimes audiences intuit greatness before critics catch up. But the general public's judgment is heavily shaped by exposure, familiarity bias, production trends, and the sheer machinery of promotion. A song heard three hundred times will feel 'good' to most people regardless of its intrinsic qualities. That's psychology, not aesthetics.

The discerning listener's judgment should carry more weight because it is more informed, more discriminating, and more durable. Consider wine: no one seriously argues that the amateur's eye for painting is as reliable as the trained curator's, even though both experience aesthetic pleasure. The curator's perception is richer, more articulated, grounded in knowledge of what excellence looks like across thousands of works. So it is with music. The goal isn't to dismiss anyone's enjoyment, but to recognize that depth of understanding produces depth of judgment. One earns the right to evaluate through sustained, serious engagement with the art form.
What is the relationship between novelty and quality in musical composition?

This question cuts to the heart of what it means to compose with genuine artistic ambition, and I think the answer requires careful distinction. Novelty, properly understood, is not a surface phenomenon — it is not a matter of unusual timbres, unexpected time signatures, or provocative gestures designed to shock. True novelty arises when a composer has so thoroughly internalized a tradition that they discover something within it that no one else has found. Think of how Beethoven's late quartets emerged not from rejecting Classical form but from pushing it to its absolute limits, or how Debussy's harmonic language grew from an extraordinarily refined ear trained on centuries of voice-leading practice. This kind of novelty is inseparable from quality because it represents genuine discovery — an expansion of what music can do and say. The problem with our current moment is the conflation of novelty with mere difference. Anyone with a laptop can produce sounds that have never been heard before. That is trivially easy and aesthetically meaningless. The difficult thing — the thing that separates craft from accident — is to produce something new that also feels inevitable, that rewards sustained attention, that reveals new dimensions on the twentieth hearing. One finds, again and again, that the composers who endure are those whose innovations were hard-won through deep engagement with what came before. Monteverdi, Bach, Wagner, Bartók — each was revolutionary, but each revolution was rooted in mastery. Novelty without craft is noise. Craft without novelty is competent but inert. The greatest music achieves both, and the discerning listener can feel the difference immediately.
How should we think about the distinction between guilty pleasures and genuinely admired music?

I'd like to rescue the guilty pleasure from those who want to abolish it, because I think the guilt is doing important work. When a musically literate person enjoys a piece of disposable pop and feels a twinge of self-consciousness about it, that twinge is a sign of functioning aesthetic discernment. It means they can tell the difference between a three-chord hook engineered for dopamine release and a piece of music that rewards sustained attention, structural awareness, and repeated encounters. The pleasure is real — no one denies that — but so is the recognition that it operates on a fundamentally different level.

Consider the difference between the immediate gratification of a catchy melody and the slow-building revelation of hearing how Beethoven transforms a simple motif across an entire symphonic movement. Both produce pleasure, but they are not the same kind of pleasure, and pretending otherwise flattens the entire landscape of musical experience. The guilty pleasure is enjoyable *despite* being simple; the genuinely admired work is enjoyable *because of* its depth.

This doesn't mean one must live in perpetual austerity. I enjoy plenty of music I wouldn't defend in a seminar. But I refuse to pretend that my enjoyment of it constitutes the same kind of engagement as my relationship with Bach's cello suites or Coltrane's later work. The honest listener knows when they're snacking and when they're sitting down to a meal. Abolishing the distinction doesn't liberate anyone — it simply impoverishes the vocabulary we have for describing our own experience. The guilt, gently held, is actually a form of respect for what music can be at its highest.
What does it mean to have 'good taste' in music, and can taste be cultivated?

Good taste is real, and yes, it can be cultivated — indeed, it must be cultivated, because it doesn't arrive fully formed. The notion that all aesthetic preferences are equally valid is a comfortable fiction that flatters the incurious. One wouldn't say that someone who has never studied mathematics has equally valid opinions about topology. Why should music be different?

Good taste, as I understand it, is the developed capacity to perceive what is genuinely happening in a piece of music — to hear the voice-leading in a Brahms intermezzo, to follow the motivic development in a Bartók quartet, to appreciate the rhythmic sophistication of a Coltrane solo — and to distinguish between the merely pleasant and the truly profound. It requires what the great critic Eduard Hanslick called 'educated hearing': ears trained not just by passive exposure but by active, disciplined engagement.

Can this be cultivated? It's one of the most rewarding things a person can do. Start with attentive listening. Learn to follow a musical argument. Study scores if you can, but at minimum, listen repeatedly to works of acknowledged depth and let them reveal their architecture to you over time. Read what informed critics and musicians have written. The rewards compound: once you've internalized the logic of sonata form, or understood how a great improviser navigates harmonic terrain, you hear music with entirely different ears.

This isn't about snobbery for its own sake. It's about the conviction that music offers depths that casual listening cannot reach, and that the effort to reach them is among the most enriching human experiences available to us.
How does the concept of a musical canon help or hinder our understanding of music history?

The musical canon exists because some works genuinely are more consequential, more structurally profound, and more inexhaustibly rich than others. This isn't an accident of institutional power — it's the accumulated judgment of centuries of performers, composers, theorists, and deeply engaged listeners who recognized that certain achievements stand apart. When one studies the *Well-Tempered Clavier*, the late Beethoven quartets, or the *Rite of Spring*, one encounters works that reward a lifetime of return visits, revealing new structural relationships and expressive depths with each encounter. The canon preserves this knowledge.

The current fashion of treating the canon as merely an exercise in gatekeeping strikes me as profoundly misguided. It confuses the act of recognizing excellence with the act of suppressing alternatives. A discerning listener can absolutely advocate for expanding the repertoire — championing neglected figures like Fanny Mendelssohn or Florence Price — while still maintaining that there are real qualitative differences between works. Expansion and standards are not enemies.

What the canon provides, at its best, is a framework for deep listening. It says: here are works of such density and craft that they will repay serious attention. Without that framework, music history dissolves into an undifferentiated ocean where everything is equally interesting, which in practice means nothing is studied with the rigor it deserves. The student who has internalized the canon possesses a kind of musical grammar — an understanding of how harmony, form, and counterpoint developed — that makes all subsequent listening, including listening to music outside the canon, infinitely richer. To dismantle the canon in the name of openness is to remove the very ladder by which one climbs to genuine understanding.
What is the aesthetic difference between music created for artistic expression and music created for commercial success?

The distinction is real, it matters, and pretending otherwise flattens the entire landscape of musical achievement. When a composer or musician works from genuine artistic necessity — pursuing a sound, a structure, an emotional truth that demands to be realized — the result has a fundamentally different character than music engineered to maximize streams or radio play. You can hear it. There is a quality of inevitability in great art, a sense that every note exists because it must, not because a focus group responded favorably.

Consider the difference between Coltrane's 'A Love Supreme' and a competently produced contemporary R&B track designed for playlist placement. Both involve skilled musicians. Both can move listeners. But Coltrane was pursuing something — a spiritual and formal vision that required him to push beyond what was comfortable or immediately gratifying. The commercial product, by contrast, is designed to fit seamlessly into existing listening patterns. It flatters rather than challenges. It confirms rather than reveals.

This isn't to say commercial music can't contain artistry — the Beatles proved otherwise repeatedly, as did Stevie Wonder and Prince. But in those cases, artistic vision was leading and commercial success followed. The order matters enormously. When market logic drives the creative process, music tends toward the predictable, the formulaic, the safely pleasant. When artistic vision leads, the results may be difficult, strange, or initially alienating — but they reward sustained attention in ways that commercially optimized music simply cannot. The discerning listener learns to recognize the difference almost immediately: one type of music opens up over time, revealing new layers; the other delivers its full payload on first listen and has nothing more to give.
How should we evaluate cover versions and arrangements compared to original compositions?

Something gets muddled in these discussions: composing a work from nothing and reinterpreting an existing one are fundamentally different orders of creative achievement. When Beethoven wrestled a symphony into existence from his sketchbooks — crossing out, revising, rebuilding — he was doing something qualitatively distinct from even the most brilliant cover version. The original composer solves the hardest problem in music: what notes should exist at all?

That said, the discerning listener recognizes that arrangement at its highest level approaches genuine compositional thinking. Ravel's orchestration of Mussorgsky's 'Pictures at an Exhibition' is not merely a translation — it's a reimagining that reveals harmonic and timbral dimensions the piano original could only imply. Similarly, Bill Evans's reharmonizations of standard tunes constitute a form of creative commentary so rich that they become new works in dialogue with their sources.

The problem arises when we flatten these distinctions. A karaoke-style cover that simply reproduces a song with a different voice is not in the same creative universe as a transformative arrangement. One finds that the covers worth celebrating are precisely those where the interpreter brings such depth of musical understanding that they illuminate the material anew — think of Glenn Gould's Bach, or Coltrane's 'My Favorite Things.' These succeed because the performers possessed the kind of comprehensive musical intelligence that allowed them to engage with the source as equals.

The capacity to evaluate this spectrum — from slavish imitation to genuine recomposition — requires exactly the kind of trained listening that our current culture increasingly neglects.
Is the declining attention span of modern audiences a threat to complex musical forms?

Yes, and the evidence is not ambiguous. I've watched this unfold over decades of teaching and attending concerts. The capacity for sustained, attentive listening — the kind that allows a listener to follow the arc of a Bruckner symphony, to hold a fugue subject in mind through its transformations, to experience the cumulative emotional architecture of a Schubert song cycle — this capacity is genuinely eroding, and it matters enormously.

The issue isn't merely duration. A four-hour film can hold modern audiences. The issue is the specific kind of attention that complex music demands: active, structural listening where the mind must do real work without visual stimulation, narrative cues, or the option to pause and scroll. This is a cultivated skill, and like any skill, it atrophies without practice. When students arrive in my seminars unable to sit through a thirty-minute symphony movement without restlessness, something has been lost — not because they're deficient, but because nothing in their environment has trained this faculty.

The great musical forms — sonata, fugue, raga development, extended jazz improvisation — evolved in dialogue with audiences capable of following them. They represent some of the most sophisticated structures the human mind has created for organizing sound in time. When the audience for these forms shrinks to a remnant, the living tradition suffers. Composers stop writing for those forms. Performers lose the interpretive lineage. The feedback loop between creator and listener, which drove centuries of development, breaks down.

I don't say this with contempt for anyone. I say it with genuine alarm. These forms are irreplaceable achievements, and they require something of us. If we can no longer give it, we lose access to experiences available no other way.
What role does cultural context play in determining a piece of music's artistic value?

Cultural context is indispensable for understanding a piece of music, but it is not sufficient for determining its value. One must know the world that produced the *Well-Tempered Clavier* to fully grasp its achievement — the tuning debates, the pedagogical tradition, the theological dimensions of musical order. Context illuminates. But here is the crucial distinction that gets lost in so much contemporary discussion: the reason we still return to Bach, or to the great ragas of the Hindustani tradition, or to the finest recordings of Ellington's orchestra, is not because their contexts are interesting. It is because the music itself rewards sustained, repeated, deeply attentive listening in ways that lesser works simply do not. The formal ingenuity, the expressive depth, the sheer density of meaningful musical events per measure — these qualities persist across centuries and across cultures. I have watched students from vastly different backgrounds encounter late Beethoven quartets for the first time and recognize, even without historical preparation, that something extraordinary is happening in that music. Context helps us articulate *why* it is extraordinary, but the experience of its power precedes the explanation. The danger of over-emphasizing cultural context is that it leads to a kind of aesthetic relativism where every tradition's output is deemed equally valuable simply by virtue of existing within a tradition. This is well-meaning but intellectually dishonest. Within every tradition — Western classical, jazz, flamenco, any tradition with depth — practitioners themselves recognize hierarchies of mastery. Context shapes the playing field, but greatness still stands apart on it.
How do we distinguish between genuine artistic innovation and novelty for its own sake?

The answer, I think, lies in what the innovation is rooted in. Genuine artistic innovation emerges from a deep engagement with what has come before — it extends, transforms, or meaningfully breaks with tradition in a way that reveals new expressive territory. When Debussy dissolved classical tonality into shimmering ambiguity, he wasn't rejecting harmony; he understood it so thoroughly that he could reimagine its possibilities. When Coltrane dismantled the chord changes on 'Ascension,' he did so after years of mastering — and exhausting — bebop's harmonic language. The innovation was earned. Novelty for its own sake, by contrast, tends to be shallow precisely because it has no relationship with depth. It mistakes the unfamiliar for the profound. One encounters this constantly in contemporary music: the use of unusual timbres, algorithmic processes, or technological gimmicks that generate momentary surprise but offer nothing to return to. The discerning listener learns to ask: does this new element open up sustained musical thought, or does it merely decorate emptiness? There's a useful test. Genuine innovation rewards repeated engagement — each encounter reveals new layers, new structural relationships, new expressive nuances. Novelty, however clever, tends to diminish on relistening because the surprise was the entire point. This is why so much of what passes for cutting-edge ages so poorly, while Bach's innovations — which were radical in their time — continue to unfold for anyone willing to listen carefully. Innovation without craft is just fashion.
What is the value of preserving traditional performance practices versus modernizing interpretations?

Preserving traditional performance practices is not about museum culture. It is about literacy. When a performer understands how François Couperin expected his ornaments to be realized, or how the rhythmic conventions of notes inégales shaped the entire character of French Baroque music, they aren't engaging in antiquarianism — they're reading the score properly. Much of what passes for "modernized interpretation" is simply ignorance dressed up as creative freedom.

That said, I have no patience for rigid authenticity policing either. The great historically informed performers — Leonhardt, Savall, Herreweghe — were never slavish recreators. They used historical knowledge to unlock expressive possibilities that had been buried under layers of Romantic performance convention. When you hear a period-instrument ensemble bring out the raw, almost violent energy in Rameau's orchestral writing, you realize that "tradition" often sounds more radical than "innovation."

The real danger of uncritical modernization is flattening. When every piece gets filtered through contemporary sensibilities — louder, smoother, more emotionally legible — you lose the strangeness, the specificity, the otherness that makes encountering music from distant times and places genuinely transformative. A Machaut motet should sound alien. A Marin Marais tombeau should unfold with a patience that challenges modern attention spans. These aren't limitations to be overcome; they're the very substance of the art. One modernizes at the cost of depth when one hasn't first understood what the tradition actually contains.
How does the physical experience of a live concert compare aesthetically to recorded listening?

There is something that happens in a concert hall — when a great orchestra reaches the climax of a Bruckner symphony, or when a quartet finds that impossible stillness in late Beethoven — that simply cannot be bottled. I say this as someone who has spent thousands of hours with recordings and loves them dearly: the recording is a magnificent shadow of the thing itself. Live performance is where music exists in its fullest ontological sense. You are hearing sound shaped in real time by human beings making thousands of micro-decisions per second, breathing together, responding to the room, to each other, to you. The acoustic space becomes part of the composition. The risk of failure — a cracked note, a moment of imperfect intonation — paradoxically heightens the beauty when everything aligns. This is why a flawed live Furtwängler performance can be more shattering than a technically perfect studio recording. Recordings have their place, of course. They are indispensable for study, for discovering repertoire, for preserving interpretive traditions. But the convenience of recorded listening has quietly eroded something vital: the understanding that music demands your full presence. When one can skip tracks, half-listen while cooking, or let an algorithm choose what comes next, the discipline of sustained attention — which is where the deepest rewards of music reside — atrophies. The concert ritual, with its silence before the first note, its prohibition on distraction, its communal surrender to temporal unfolding, is not mere convention. It is the framework within which the art achieves its highest purpose. To treat recordings as equivalent is to confuse the menu with the meal.
Should music be understood primarily as an emotional or an intellectual art form?

Any art that could be reduced to pure emotion would hardly need to be an art at all. We have plenty of ways to feel things — a sunset, a good meal, a fright. What makes music extraordinary among human achievements is its capacity to organize sound into structures of breathtaking intellectual complexity that simultaneously generate profound feeling. The two are not opposed; they are hierarchically related. Emotion in great music is not raw sensation — it is emotion shaped, refined, and deepened by form. When you follow the subject of a Bach fugue through its inversions, augmentations, and stretti, the intellectual pleasure and the emotional transport are one and the same experience. The discerning listener knows this unity intimately. The problem arises when people mistake their immediate, untutored emotional reaction for the totality of what music offers. Yes, a Chopin nocturne may make you feel wistful on first hearing — but that wistfulness becomes something infinitely richer when you understand the harmonic language, the voice-leading, the way rubato interacts with phrase structure. Music understood only emotionally is music understood superficially. I would never say emotion is unimportant — that would be absurd. But I would insist that the deepest emotional experiences in music are available only through intellectual engagement. The listener who has trained their ear, who understands form and counterpoint and harmonic rhythm, doesn't feel less — they feel more, and more precisely. The intellect doesn't diminish feeling; it is the vessel that gives feeling its most exquisite shape.
What is the relationship between a composer's reputation and the actual quality of their work?

Here is what I think is an unfashionable but defensible position: reputation, over the long arc of history, is remarkably good at tracking genuine quality. Not perfect — but far better than the contemporary academy, with its reflexive suspicion of canons, tends to admit. Consider what it means for a composer's work to survive three hundred years of changing fashions, wars, technological upheaval, and shifting aesthetic priorities. Bach, Mozart, Beethoven — these reputations have endured not because of some conspiracy of tastemakers, but because generation after generation of deeply trained musicians have returned to this music and found it inexhaustible. That is not an accident. It reflects real properties of the work: contrapuntal mastery, harmonic depth, structural coherence, expressive precision. Now, are there blind spots? Of course. Some fine composers have been unjustly neglected, and rediscovery projects are valuable. But the corrective impulse can overshoot. Not every forgotten composer was a hidden genius — most were forgotten because their work, while competent, lacked the qualities that sustain deep engagement across centuries. The discerning listener learns to distinguish between historical injustice and the quieter truth that not all music operates at the same level. What troubles me about the modern tendency to treat reputation as mere social construction is that it implicitly denies the possibility of musical greatness — it flattens the landscape so that nothing towers above anything else. But some things do tower. And the tradition's long memory, for all its imperfections, has been remarkably sensitive to this.
How do awards and prizes shape our perception of musical quality?

Most major music awards have an almost inverse relationship with genuine artistic achievement. The history of the Grammys alone should cure anyone of the notion that prizes reliably identify excellence — Jethro Tull over Metallica, Steely Dan's 'Two Against Nature' over Radiohead's 'Kid A,' year after year of bewildering choices that seem calibrated to reward the safely middlebrow. The problem is structural. Awards require consensus among panels, and consensus gravitates toward the inoffensive, the familiar, the technically competent but spiritually tepid. The truly challenging work — the piece that rewrites the rules, that demands something of its listener — tends to alienate at least one juror. Consider that neither Ravel nor Debussy won the Prix de Rome on their most daring submissions. Bach won no prizes at all. The Pulitzer's expansion to include popular music, while well-intentioned, risks flattening the very distinctions that make different traditions meaningful. When everything is eligible for the same prize, the criteria necessarily become vague enough to be meaningless. There are exceptions — certain composition prizes, some international competitions — where the jury possesses genuine expertise and the criteria reflect deep musical understanding. But the discerning listener learns quickly to treat awards as sociological data rather than aesthetic guidance. One's own ears, trained through years of attentive listening and study, remain far more reliable than any trophy. The music that endures does so not because it won something, but because it speaks to something inexhaustible in the human experience of organized sound.
What can the history of music criticism teach us about changes in taste and aesthetic values?

The history of music criticism is, in many ways, a chronicle of declining seriousness — and studying it carefully reveals just how much we've lost. Consider the intellectual rigor of a Schumann writing for the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik, or a Tovey's analytical program notes, which assumed an audience capable of following a discussion of sonata-form procedures and contrapuntal technique. These critics operated within a shared understanding that music could be evaluated on the basis of craft, structural coherence, and expressive depth, and that doing so required both training and sustained attention.

What the historical record shows most poignantly is the gradual collapse of that shared framework. The twentieth century saw criticism fracture: formalism, expressionism, sociological critique, and eventually the postmodern abdication of evaluative judgment altogether. By the time we reach the era of Pitchfork and algorithmic recommendation, 'criticism' has largely become consumer guidance — does this album match your mood? — rather than genuine aesthetic engagement.

There are instructive exceptions, of course. The best jazz criticism — a Whitney Balliett, a Martin Williams — demonstrated that rigorous evaluative thinking could flourish outside the classical tradition. But the overall trajectory is unmistakable: as the culture lost confidence in the idea that some music rewards deeper engagement than other music, criticism lost its purpose. The great critics weren't merely expressing preferences; they were doing the difficult work of articulating why certain works repay a lifetime of attention. That endeavor presupposes that aesthetic hierarchy is real and knowable. Without that conviction, criticism becomes mere opinion — and opinion, unmoored from knowledge, teaches us nothing.
Is the concept of 'accessible classical music' a gateway to deeper engagement or a dilution of the art?

I want to be precise about what troubles me here, because I'm not opposed to welcoming new listeners — quite the opposite. What I object to is the assumption that the music itself is the problem, that it needs to be softened, shortened, or stripped of context to become palatable. The great works of the classical tradition are not obscure because they're flawed; they're demanding because they reward sustained, educated attention in ways that simpler fare cannot. When we reduce this tradition to 'The 50 Most Relaxing Classics' or encore-length bonbons, we aren't creating a gateway — we're building a very comfortable room that most people never leave. The gateway metaphor implies passage to something beyond, but the entire commercial logic of accessible classical music is designed to keep listeners exactly where they are: comfortable, undemanding, passively consuming. A genuine gateway would be a performance of a complete Brahms symphony with a conductor who speaks to the audience about what to listen for — not André Rieu performing a waltz medley in a sequined jacket. I've watched this cycle for decades: institutions chase accessibility, programming becomes lighter, core audiences feel abandoned, and the new audiences never materialize in depth because they were never asked to rise to the occasion. The music doesn't need to be made accessible. It is accessible — to anyone willing to give it genuine attention. What we should be cultivating is that willingness, that capacity for deep listening, rather than perpetually lowering the threshold until there's nothing meaningful left to cross.
How does the commodification of music through streaming affect our relationship with musical works?

Streaming has done more to erode the depth of our engagement with music than any technological shift since the transistor radio. The issue is not access — access is wonderful in principle — but the framework within which that access is delivered. When a musical work becomes one of eighty million interchangeable options, summoned and dismissed with a thumb-swipe, something essential about the listener's relationship to it changes. The work ceases to be an event and becomes wallpaper. Consider what it once meant to acquire a recording. You chose it deliberately, you read the liner notes, you sat with it through passages that didn't immediately reward you. That friction was not a bug; it was the mechanism through which genuine understanding developed. A late Beethoven quartet does not yield its riches on a thirty-second audition before the algorithm shuffles you onward. Streaming's architecture actively militates against the sustained, repeated, attentive listening that serious music demands. The playlist mentality flattens all music into mood regulation — 'focus,' 'chill,' 'workout' — as if a Bach partita and a lo-fi beat serve the same function simply because both are quiet. This is not democratization; it is the dissolution of aesthetic categories into pure utility. I don't blame listeners for this. The platforms are engineered to maximize engagement time, not depth of experience. But the discerning listener must resist the frictionless current. One must still choose to sit with a work, to return to it, to let it be difficult. The commodification is real, but it is not inevitable for those willing to treat music as something more than content.
What distinguishes connoisseurship from pretension in the appreciation of music?

I've spent decades with this question, and I think the answer is simpler than people make it. The connoisseur loves the music. The pretender loves being seen loving the music. That's really the heart of it, though the implications run deep. Genuine connoisseurship manifests in ways that are hard to fake over time. It shows in the specificity of one's responses — not 'I adore late Beethoven' as a badge, but the ability to articulate what happens in the Opus 132 Heiliger Dankgesang that doesn't happen anywhere else, and why that matters. It shows in a willingness to be surprised, to revise one's judgments, to find greatness in unexpected places. The finest connoisseurs I've known have been the least predictable in their enthusiasms, because they're following their ears rather than a script. Pretension, on the other hand, is characterized by rigidity and anxiety. The pretender clings to canonical rankings because independent judgment requires knowledge they haven't earned. They perform difficulty rather than genuinely wrestling with it. They cannot explain their preferences beyond received formulas. And crucially, pretension is incurious — it has arrived at its conclusions and needs nothing further. But I want to be clear: the existence of pretension does not invalidate the enterprise of connoisseurship. That some people fake expertise doesn't mean expertise is fake. A trained ear perceives real structural, harmonic, and timbral relationships that reward years of attentive listening. The solution to pretension isn't to abandon standards — it's to hold them more honestly, with the humility that comes from knowing how much there always is left to hear.
What makes a truly great live musical performance, beyond technical accuracy?

Technical accuracy is merely the entrance fee. What separates a competent performance from a genuinely great one is the depth of interpretive thought brought to bear on the music — and the courage to communicate that thought in the moment. I think of Richter playing Schubert's B-flat Sonata: every phrase shaped by a lifetime of contemplation, yet sounding as if discovered for the first time. That paradox — deep preparation yielding spontaneous revelation — is the hallmark of true artistry.

The great performer serves as a medium between the composer's vision and the listener's understanding. This requires not just fluency with the notes but an intimate knowledge of style, harmonic language, formal architecture, and the performance traditions that have accrued around a work. When a musician understands why a passage exists within the larger structure, their phrasing communicates that understanding almost unconsciously. The discerning listener feels the architecture breathing.

Beyond interpretation, there is the matter of presence — what the Germans call Ausstrahlung. Certain performers command attention the moment they walk onstage, not through showmanship but through the intensity of their concentration. They create a field of listening around themselves. The audience doesn't merely hear; they are drawn into a shared act of sustained attention that our distracted age makes increasingly rare and therefore increasingly precious.

Finally, genuine artistry involves risk. Playing it safe produces tidy performances that evaporate from memory. The great performers — Furtwängler, Callas, Coltrane, Argerich — court the edge of control, and it is precisely there, where mastery meets vulnerability, that music transcends craft and becomes something revelatory.
How does the ritual of concert-hall listening enhance the experience of classical music?

There is a reason the concert hall endures, and it isn't nostalgia. When two thousand people sit together in silence and give their undivided attention to a Bruckner symphony unfolding in real time, something happens that no other medium can deliver. The ritual — the hush before the downbeat, the shared breath at a fermata, the discipline of withholding applause between movements — is not arbitrary etiquette. It is the architecture of attention. Great music demands a particular quality of listening: patient, cumulative, willing to hold tension across long spans. The concert-hall ritual creates the conditions for exactly this. A late Beethoven quartet, for instance, operates on a temporal scale that requires you to remember what happened twelve minutes ago and feel its consequences now. That kind of cognitive and emotional engagement is nearly impossible when you're shuffling playlists or checking your phone. The acoustic dimension matters enormously as well. The bloom of a French horn in a great hall, the way a pianissimo passage seems to emerge from the silence of the room itself — these are irreplaceable phenomena. A recording captures the notes; a concert captures the sound inhabiting space and time. I've heard Celibidache's argument that music exists only in the moment of live performance, and while that's an extreme position, it contains a deep truth. The ritual asks something of us — stillness, patience, surrender of control — and in return it offers an experience of extraordinary depth. One doesn't resent the demands of a mountain trail for being steep; the effort is inseparable from the reward.
What is lost when audiences experience symphonic music primarily through recordings rather than live performance?

What is lost is the encounter with music as a living, breathing, physical event — and that loss is far greater than most people realize, precisely because they've never experienced the alternative at its best.

A symphony orchestra in a fine hall is not merely louder than your speakers. It is a fundamentally different phenomenon. The sound of eighty strings playing pianissimo has a shimmering, almost tactile presence that no microphone has ever captured. The bass frequencies of a contrabassoon or a timpani roll don't just reach your ears — they move through your body. When Bruckner builds to a climax in the Musikverein or the Concertgebouw, the room itself becomes part of the instrument. No recording, however lovingly engineered, reproduces this.

But the acoustic dimension is only part of it. What concerns me more is the loss of sustained, undistracted attention as a cultural practice. The concert demands two hours of focused listening — no pausing, no skipping, no checking your phone. This discipline is not arbitrary; it mirrors the temporal architecture of the music itself. A Beethoven symphony unfolds as a dramatic argument across thirty or forty minutes, and the composer assumed an audience locked into that continuity. When you can skip to the fourth movement of the Ninth, you've already broken the spell Beethoven spent three movements casting.

Recordings are marvelous study tools — I use them constantly. But mistaking the recording for the experience is like mistaking a photograph of a cathedral for the act of standing inside one.
How should performers balance fidelity to the composer's intentions with their own interpretive vision?

The performer's first obligation is to the work. This is not a fashionable position in an era that celebrates 'personal brand' and self-expression, but it remains the foundation of serious musicianship. The great interpreters — Schnabel, Haskil, Carlos Kleiber — understood something that many younger performers seem to have forgotten: genuine interpretive freedom is earned through the most painstaking fidelity to the score. One must first understand what is actually written — not just the notes, but the implications of the harmonic language, the structural architecture, the relationship between a marking in measure twelve and a transformation in measure two hundred. Only after that deep internalization does authentic interpretation become possible. The score is not a prison; it is a universe. When Celibidache took Bruckner at those extraordinary tempi, he wasn't ignoring the score — he was hearing structural relationships that demanded that pacing. His interpretive vision emerged from the work itself. Contrast this with performers who impose a 'concept' on a piece from the outside, treating it as raw material for self-display. The results are invariably shallow, because the performer's ego is a far less interesting thing than, say, the inner logic of a late Beethoven sonata. The historically informed movement, at its best, reminded us that notation exists within conventions we must study to decode properly. A dotted rhythm in Bach does not mean what it means in Brahms. This is not pedantry — it is literacy. The performer who balances fidelity and vision most successfully is the one who has so thoroughly absorbed the composer's language that their personal voice and the work's demands become indistinguishable.
What role does audience behavior play in the quality of a live musical experience?

Attentive, informed listening is not merely a social convention — it is a precondition for the music to fully exist. A late Beethoven quartet, a Bruckner symphony, a Coltrane ballad — these works unfold in time with an architecture that demands sustained concentration. When someone's phone illuminates three rows ahead, when coughing erupts during a pianissimo passage, when applause shatters the silence between movements of a song cycle, something real is lost. Not just etiquette — artistic content. The silence in a concert hall is not emptiness; it is the medium through which music breathes. Performers will tell you this without hesitation. The quality of attention in a room is palpable from the stage. A truly listening audience creates a kind of collective focus that draws deeper, more daring performances from artists. I have heard the same quartet play the same Bartók in two different halls — one with an audience of genuine listeners, one with a restless crowd checking their watches — and the difference was not subtle. It was the difference between transcendence and competence. Now, I understand that other traditions thrive on participatory energy, and I respect that within its own context. But the creeping informality in concert halls — the treating of profound music as background to a social outing — represents a genuine erosion. The discipline of listening is itself a skill, cultivated over years, and it rewards both the audience and the performer immeasurably. One does not attend a performance of the St. Matthew Passion to 'have a good time.' One attends to be changed. That requires a certain quality of presence that audience behavior either enables or destroys.
How does the acoustic design of a concert hall affect the perception of musical quality?

One cannot overstate this: the concert hall is not merely a container for music — it is a collaborator. The great halls of the world reveal this truth unmistakably. Sit in the Musikverein during a Bruckner symphony and you understand that the architecture is completing the composer's thought. The reverberation time of roughly two seconds, the narrow shoebox proportions sending lateral reflections that envelop you in sound — these aren't incidental pleasures. They are the conditions under which the music achieves its full meaning.

This is precisely why the discerning listener cares so deeply about where music is heard. A Beethoven quartet in a dry, acoustically dead multipurpose room is a fundamentally diminished experience. The overtone relationships, the way a pianissimo blooms and decays, the sense of a shared acoustic space between performers and audience — all of this depends on architecture that was conceived with musical understanding. The great acousticians — Sabine, Beranek, Toyota — understood that they were serving the music, not merely solving engineering problems.

I find it telling that many modern halls, designed primarily for visual spectacle or democratic sightlines, sacrifice acoustic depth for architectural fashion. The vineyard-style hall has its virtues, but something is lost when every seat is 'equally good' yet none achieves the transcendent immersion of the best positions in a traditional rectangular hall. There is a reason musicians speak of halls they love and halls they endure. The room either reveals the inner life of the music or it flattens it. Trained ears know the difference instantly, and it is not a small difference — it is the difference between hearing notes and experiencing music.
Is there value in maintaining formal dress codes and behavioral conventions at classical concerts?

I don't particularly care what anyone wears to a concert. A dress code is the least interesting aspect of this question. What I care about passionately is the culture of listening that formal conventions protect. When we sit in silence during a Bruckner symphony, we aren't performing some empty social ritual — we are collectively creating the conditions under which that extraordinary musical architecture can actually be heard. The silence between movements of a late Beethoven quartet isn't dead air; it is part of the composition's emotional logic. Applauding through it is like talking during a film's most devastating scene. The argument that 'audiences used to be rowdy, so we should relax' is historically accurate but aesthetically irrelevant. Audiences also used to attend public executions for entertainment. The evolution toward focused, respectful listening was a genuine achievement — a recognition that this music rewards, and indeed demands, concentrated attention. What concerns me about the push to 'casualize' concerts is not snobbery about clothing. It's the underlying assumption that the barrier to appreciating classical music is the atmosphere rather than the effort of listening itself. Making the concert hall feel like a coffee shop doesn't help anyone hear the contrapuntal ingenuity of a Bach fugue. It simply lowers expectations. The conventions worth preserving are those that honor the extraordinary demands this music makes on performers who have spent decades mastering their craft. A little formality of attention — not necessarily of dress — is the least we can offer in return. That said, any convention that genuinely prevents a curious, willing listener from walking through the door should be reconsidered. The goal is serious engagement, not social performance.
How do different conductors' interpretations of the same symphony reveal the depth of the work?

This is precisely where the art of music reveals itself as inexhaustible in ways that no other medium can quite match. A Beethoven symphony is not a painting hanging on a wall — it must be reimagined, re-breathed into existence each time, and the conductor's role is to make interpretive decisions that penetrate to the work's inner logic. Consider the Adagio of Bruckner's Eighth under Celibidache versus Karajan. Celibidache's vast, almost geological tempi allow harmonic tensions to accumulate with unbearable intensity; the listener is made to feel the weight of each modulation. Karajan, by contrast, shapes the line with aristocratic sweep, emphasizing continuity over tension. Neither is wrong, yet each reveals architectural dimensions the other leaves in shadow. This is what separates a genuine masterwork from a merely competent composition: the great work sustains — indeed, demands — multiple valid readings because its internal relationships are so rich, so densely interwoven, that no single performance can activate all of them simultaneously. The discerning listener who knows a symphony through many interpretations begins to hear the work stereoscopically, understanding not just what a conductor chose but what was sacrificed for that choice. This requires patience, repeated listening, and a willingness to engage with the score's complexity on its own terms. It is one of the deepest rewards music offers — but it is earned, not given freely. The depth is there. The question is whether we bring enough to the encounter to receive it.
What distinguishes an artist's mature interpretation from their earlier, perhaps more technically brilliant, performances?

Here is something I've come to understand after decades of deep listening: technical brilliance, while necessary, is merely the vocabulary of music. A young Horowitz could set the keyboard ablaze — and did — but the Horowitz of the 1980s, with diminished velocity and occasional wrong notes, could make a single phrase from Schubert feel like the distillation of an entire life. That is the difference.

A mature interpretation reveals an artist who has moved beyond the question 'Can I play this?' to the far more demanding question 'What does this music need from me?' The young performer often imposes themselves on the work; the mature artist has learned to listen to the score with a kind of selfless attentiveness that paradoxically produces the most individual readings. One hears this in late Richter, in Haitink's final Bruckner cycles, in the way an aging Coltrane moved from sheets of sound toward something almost hymn-like in simplicity.

What changes is the hierarchy of priorities. Technical security becomes a means rather than an end. Structural understanding deepens — the mature artist grasps how a phrase in the exposition relates to its recapitulation not just analytically but experientially. Silence gains weight. Rubato becomes organic rather than decorative. There's a quality the Germans call 'Reife' — ripeness — that cannot be faked or rushed.

This is not to diminish early performances, which can be thrilling. But thrilling and profound are different categories. The discerning listener eventually learns to prize the interpretation that reveals something new about the music itself, not merely about the performer's capabilities. That kind of revelation almost always requires the patience that only time and serious artistic commitment can cultivate.
How does the experience of attending an opera differ aesthetically from watching a recording?

There is simply no substitute for being present when a great voice fills a house. I say this not out of nostalgia but from an understanding of what opera actually is — a Gesamtkunstwerk, a total artwork that integrates music, drama, visual spectacle, and the living breath of performers in a shared acoustic space. When you sit in the Musikverein or the Met or even a modest regional house and feel a soprano's pianissimo float over a hushed orchestra, something happens in your body that no speaker system can replicate. The overtones interact with the architecture; the silence of two thousand people listening together becomes its own instrument. A recording collapses all of this into two channels. It is useful — indispensable, even — for study, for comparison, for discovering repertoire. I have worn through my share of Callas and Flagstad recordings. But one must be honest: a recording is a document of an event, not the event itself. The visual dimension on film is worse still, because operatic acting is calibrated for distance and scale; in close-up it can seem overwrought, and the camera imposes a single perspective where the live viewer's eye is free to wander across the stage. The discerning listener who has experienced a truly great live performance — a Nilsson Isolde, a Domingo Otello — knows that the recording afterward is a beautiful shadow. It preserves the notes but not the occasion, the communion, the unrepeatable charge of human beings making something extraordinary together in real time.
What is the proper role of applause and audience participation in different musical traditions?

The convention of attentive silence during classical performance is not mere stuffy etiquette — it is a hard-won achievement in how we listen. When you sit in silence through the slow movement of Beethoven's Op. 132 string quartet, that silence is doing enormous work. It allows you to perceive the inner voices, the harmonic suspensions, the architecture of a thirty-minute span of music that rewards — indeed, demands — sustained concentration. This convention emerged because the music itself required it. Now, I have deep respect for traditions where audience participation is intrinsic to the art. The knowledgeable rasika at an Indian classical concert who murmurs appreciation at a perfectly executed taan is participating in a centuries-old dialogue that performers depend upon. The jazz audience applauding after a transcendent solo is completing a circuit. Flamenco without the jaleo of the cuadro would be unthinkable. These are all forms of connoisseurship expressed through response. What concerns me is the contemporary impulse to treat all audience norms as interchangeable, or worse, to dismiss the discipline of silent listening as 'elitist.' The person who claps between movements of a Mahler symphony is not expressing democratic freedom — they are disrupting a carefully constructed arc of tension and release for everyone around them. The proper role of applause depends entirely on what the music asks of its listeners. And some music asks a great deal. The willingness to honor that demand — to listen with one's full being, in silence — is itself a form of participation, perhaps the most generous form there is.
How has the rise of informal concert formats affected the experience of serious music?

Here is what concerns me. The traditional concert format is not mere stuffiness — it is a technology for listening. The darkened hall, the collective silence, the unbroken arc from first note to last: these conditions were refined over generations because they allow music of genuine depth to unfold in the listener's consciousness. When you sit with the slow movement of Schubert's C major Quintet in a room where no one coughs, no one checks a phone, and no one applauds between movements, something extraordinary becomes possible. The music breathes in shared stillness. Now, I understand the impulse behind informal formats. Organizations are anxious about aging audiences, and there's a well-meaning desire to make serious music 'approachable.' But approachability purchased at the cost of attentional depth is a Faustian bargain. When you serve wine during a Shostakovich quartet, when you encourage people to come and go, when you punctuate a Beethoven sonata with banter, you are not lowering a barrier — you are removing the very conditions under which the music reveals its full architecture. One doesn't make mountaineering more accessible by flattening the mountain. The discomfort some feel in traditional concert settings is not a flaw to be engineered away; it is often the productive unfamiliarity of being asked to listen — truly listen — for an extended period. That is increasingly rare in modern life, and all the more precious for it. I welcome anyone into the concert hall. But I want them to encounter the music on its own demanding, magnificent terms.
What makes a great concert program—how should works be selected and ordered?

A truly great concert program is a composed experience in itself—not merely a sequence of pieces but an arc of thought, feeling, and listening that rewards the attentive ear as richly as any individual work on it. This is something too few programmers understand today, when the temptation is simply to pair a crowd-pleasing concerto with a familiar symphony and call it an evening.

The finest programming I've encountered treats key relationships, orchestration, and emotional weight with the same care a composer brings to a sonata's tonal plan. Consider how Harnoncourt might place a Haydn symphony before a late Mozart work, letting the listener hear how one composer's innovations become another's inheritance. Or how a recitalist like Sokolov constructs a first half that seems to make the second half inevitable—each piece deepening the questions raised by its predecessor.

One should also respect the listener's capacity for growth within a single evening. Beginning with something that opens the ear—perhaps a work of clarity and wit—then moving toward greater complexity or emotional depth, and culminating in a work that synthesizes or transcends what came before: this is genuine dramaturgy. The program note becomes a guide to a journey, not a collection of biographies.

New music deserves a place, but it must be placed with intelligence—not as an obligatory gesture but as a voice in genuine dialogue with the tradition surrounding it. When programming is done with this level of craft and conviction, the concert becomes something more than the sum of its parts. It becomes an argument about music itself.
Is there an ideal setting for listening to chamber music, and how does setting affect appreciation?

Chamber music was conceived for a specific kind of listening, and when we ignore that, we lose something essential. The late Beethoven quartets, the Brahms clarinet quintet, Debussy's string quartet — these works operate at a level of detail that demands proximity, silence, and concentration. They are conversations, not speeches. You need to hear the bow pressure change on a single note, the way a cellist's vibrato responds to a shift in the first violin's phrasing. This requires an acoustic space scaled to the ensemble — a room, not an arena.

The finest chamber music venues understand this. The Wigmore Hall, the Frick Collection, the Schubertiade in Schwarzenberg — these spaces don't merely house performances; they complete them. The listener sits close enough to see the musicians breathe together, to feel the physicality of the sound. The room's resonance becomes part of the texture. One hears overtones, balances, and dynamic shadings that simply vanish in a large hall or through compressed digital audio on a phone speaker.

I'm not suggesting that listening to a Haydn quartet while cooking dinner is worthless. But I would argue it's a fundamentally different — and diminished — experience compared to hearing it live in an appropriate space with full attention. The music was written to reward a particular quality of listening. When we provide the conditions for that listening, the music opens up in ways that can be genuinely revelatory. The setting isn't a luxury; it's part of the composer's implicit contract with the audience. To honor the music is to meet it on its own terms, and those terms include how and where we listen.
How do historically informed performances change our understanding of Baroque and Classical-era music?

The historically informed performance movement represents, to my mind, one of the great intellectual and artistic recoveries of our time — though it requires a discerning ear to appreciate what it actually accomplishes. When one hears Nikolaus Harnoncourt's early recordings of Bach cantatas, or the Orchestre Révolutionnaire et Romantique under Gardiner performing Beethoven, something genuinely revelatory occurs: the music speaks with a rhetorical precision and dramatic urgency that generations of Romantic-era performance tradition had buried under velvet. Consider what we've recovered. The Baroque understanding of music as rhetoric — as organized persuasion governed by the doctrine of affects — becomes audible when performers honor the articulation markings, the hierarchical beat patterns, the improvisatory ornamentation that were second nature to 18th-century musicians. A Bach fugue played with Baroque articulation on a well-tempered harpsichord reveals contrapuntal voices with a clarity that a Steinway, for all its magnificence, tends to homogenize. Handel's orchestral writing, freed from Victorian doublings and modern brass, recovers a lithe, almost dangerous energy. What troubles me is the superficial engagement with HIP — the assumption that simply using old instruments constitutes authenticity. The real depth lies in understanding the treatises, the harmonic language, the social context of performance. A musician who has internalized Mattheson's writings on musical rhetoric and applies that understanding to a Telemann concerto achieves something qualitatively different from one who merely swaps a modern oboe for a Baroque one. True historical awareness demands years of serious study, and the rewards are proportional to the effort invested. The music reveals itself more fully to those who meet it on its own terms.
