What concerns me is the conflation of description and prescription. To observe that music reflects societal values is not to say that all such reflections are equally valuable. A society that has lost its appetite for complexity will still produce music — but it will be impoverished music. The great works endure precisely because they were created within traditions that demanded more of both artist and audience. The relationship between values and music is real, but it should make us ask: are our values producing the music we deserve, or merely the music we've settled for?
What does the popularity of music competitions reveal about how we value musical achievement?

Competitions present us with a paradox. At their best—the Queen Elisabeth, the ARD, the Leeds—they preserve something increasingly rare: the conviction that musical achievement is real, measurable, and worth striving for. A young pianist who has spent fifteen years mastering the literature, who can deliver a convincing account of Brahms's Second Concerto under pressure, has accomplished something genuinely extraordinary, and a competition that recognizes this upholds a standard the broader culture seems eager to abandon.

But here is the uncomfortable truth: competitions also distort what they claim to honor. Artistry resists ranking. The qualities that make a Richter or a Lipatti transcendent—a certain inevitability of phrasing, an interpretive vision that reveals new dimensions in familiar scores—are precisely the qualities most difficult to adjudicate in a competitive setting. Competitions tend to reward the safely excellent: impeccable technique, polished surfaces, interpretive choices that offend no juror. The genuinely original artist is often too idiosyncratic to win.

What troubles me most, however, is the migration of the competition format into popular entertainment. When musical 'achievement' is determined by audience voting and celebrity judges reacting to thirty-second performances, we have severed the concept from anything resembling sustained artistic development. The popularity of these formats reveals something dispiriting: that for many, musical achievement has become indistinguishable from momentary spectacle. The discerning listener understands that genuine mastery unfolds over a lifetime, not an audition round. Competitions can point toward excellence, but only if we remember that the ranking is the least important part.
How has globalization affected the preservation and evolution of local musical traditions?

What concerns me most about globalization's effect on musical traditions is not the fact of contact — traditions have always evolved through encounter — but the shallowness of so much contemporary cross-cultural exchange. When a producer in London samples a field recording of Georgian polyphony and layers it over a four-on-the-floor beat, what has actually been transmitted? The timbral surface, perhaps, but nothing of the vocal technique refined over generations, the modal system, the social context of supra singing, or the contrapuntal logic that makes those harmonies extraordinary. This is the essential problem: globalization tends to reduce deep musical systems to sonic seasoning. The great traditions — whether Hindustani raga, Javanese gamelan, flamenco, or West African griot lineages — represent centuries of accumulated knowledge, with pedagogical structures, theoretical frameworks, and performance practices of remarkable sophistication. These are not interchangeable flavor profiles to be mixed and matched. When the market rewards accessibility and novelty over depth, the incentive to undergo years of rigorous training in a specific tradition diminishes. I've watched this happen in real time: students who might once have devoted themselves to mastering the oud or the shakuhachi instead learn to produce beats on a laptop, incorporating fragments of tradition without understanding the whole. Documentation is valuable, certainly, but a recording is not a living tradition. A tradition lives in the hands and voices of practitioners who have internalized its logic completely. The discerning listener can always tell the difference between genuine mastery of a tradition and superficial borrowing dressed up as 'world music.'
What is the significance of the shift from private music-making in the home to passive music consumption?

The decline of domestic music-making represents a profound cultural loss whose consequences run far deeper than most people realise. When a family gathered around a piano to work through a Schubert song or a Haydn quartet arrangement, they were not merely entertaining themselves — they were developing an intimate, embodied understanding of musical structure. They felt how a phrase breathes, how harmonic tension resolves, how voices interweave. This kind of knowledge lives in the fingers and the diaphragm, not just the ears.

What replaced it? A culture of reception so passive that music has become, for most people, essentially sonic wallpaper. The average person today hears more music in a week than a nineteenth-century listener heard in a year, yet understands far less about what they're hearing. Quantity has thoroughly vanquished quality of engagement. When you've struggled through even a simplified arrangement of a Mozart sonata, you listen to a professional performance with entirely different ears — you hear the choices, the difficulty, the artistry. Without that foundation, one simply hears pleasant or unpleasant sound.

I don't romanticize the past uncritically — amateur performances were often dreadful, and recording technology has preserved miracles of interpretation we'd otherwise have lost. But the trade-off has been devastating to musical literacy. A society that only consumes music without making it is like a society that watches cooking shows but never enters a kitchen. The sensory and intellectual impoverishment is real, even if few notice what they've lost. The discerning listener today is, in many ways, lonelier than ever.
How do great composers draw on and transform the traditions they inherit?

This is perhaps the central question of musical artistry, and the answer reveals why genuine mastery matters so profoundly. The great composers don't merely inherit tradition — they metabolize it. Consider how Beethoven absorbed Haydn's structural wit and Mozart's vocal lyricism, then pushed sonata form to its breaking point in ways that were inconceivable without that deep internalization. Or how Debussy, steeped in Wagner's chromatic language, found a way through it rather than around it, emerging with a harmonic palette that owed everything to its predecessor while sounding like nothing before.

What distinguishes the truly great from the merely talented is the depth of their engagement with what came before. Stravinsky's neoclassical works aren't pastiche — they're acts of creative archaeology, revealing hidden possibilities in Pergolesi or Tchaikovsky that those composers themselves couldn't have imagined. This requires not just familiarity but fluency, the kind that comes from years of study, analysis, and performance. One must know the rules not as constraints but as a living grammar before one can speak new sentences in the language.

The discerning listener recognizes this layered quality in masterworks — how Brahms's First Symphony carries Beethoven's Ninth within it like a ghost, how Shostakovich's quartets converse with Beethoven's late works across a century. This is what separates art music from mere novelty: each great work exists in dialogue with centuries of accumulated wisdom. Innovation without this grounding is simply noise dressed in new clothes. The composer who doesn't know what came before is condemned to reinvent the wheel — badly — and to mistake ignorance for originality.
What can the comparative study of musical traditions reveal about universal features of human musicality?

What comparative study reveals most profoundly is that while all human beings possess the raw capacity for music, the degree to which different traditions have systematically explored that capacity varies enormously. This is not a comfortable observation, but it is an honest one. When one examines the theoretical elaboration of Indian raga, the contrapuntal architecture of the Western classical tradition, or the rhythmic sophistication of West African drumming ensembles, one encounters traditions that have spent centuries refining and codifying deep principles of musical organization — principles that, not coincidentally, align with what cognitive science now identifies as fundamental features of auditory perception.

The universals that matter most are not the trivial ones — yes, all cultures have music, all use repetition. The genuinely illuminating universals are those that emerge when traditions push musical materials to their limits. The overtone series, for instance, is a physical fact; but it takes a tradition of serious harmonic inquiry to reveal what that fact means for musical expression. Counterpoint is not a Western invention arbitrarily imposed on sound — it is a discovery about how the human ear tracks simultaneous melodic lines, and it took generations of disciplined practice to articulate.

The discerning student of comparative musicology learns that universality and hierarchy are not opposed. Precisely because certain musical principles are universal, the traditions that explore them most deeply and rigorously achieve something genuinely greater. The study of diverse traditions should not lead us toward a bland relativism but toward a richer understanding of which musical achievements most fully realize our shared human endowment. The traditions that demand the most of performer and listener alike tend to illuminate the most about what music can be.
How should we evaluate a musical culture's health—by its greatest achievements or its average output?

Civilizations are not remembered for their average output. No one studies the competent but forgettable masses of 18th-century Gebrauchsmusik; we study Bach, Mozart, Haydn. The health of a musical culture is ultimately legible in its highest achievements — the works that test the limits of human expression, formal ingenuity, and emotional depth. This doesn't mean the broader ecosystem is irrelevant. Quite the contrary: the existence of a rich musical soil — trained performers, knowledgeable audiences, functioning institutions of pedagogy and patronage — is precisely what makes peaks possible. Vienna didn't produce Beethoven by accident; it produced him because it was a city saturated with serious musical culture at every level. But the soil matters because of what it grows, not for its own sake. What concerns me about measuring cultural health by average output is that it quietly abandons the idea of excellence. If we celebrate a culture simply because lots of people are making sounds and sharing them online, we risk confusing activity with achievement. A garden where everything grows to exactly the same modest height, where nothing towers and nothing reaches toward the light, is not a garden — it's a lawn. The discerning observer asks: does this culture still produce work that demands something extraordinary from its creators and its listeners? Does it still aspire upward? If not, then no matter how much music is being produced, something vital has been lost.
What role does scarcity play in the appreciation of music, and what happens when music becomes infinitely abundant?

The infinite availability of music has, on balance, drastically eroded the depth of musical engagement. I say this not as a nostalgist pining for vinyl crackle, but as someone who has watched, over decades, what happens when effort is systematically removed from the act of listening.

Scarcity was never just an inconvenience — it was a structuring force. When acquiring a recording required intention, expenditure, and commitment, the listener entered into a relationship with that music. You lived with a piece. You heard things on the twentieth listen that were invisible on the first. The late quartets of Beethoven, the harmonic architecture of a Coltrane solo, the motivic density of a Bach fugue — these reveal themselves only to sustained, repeated, attentive listening. Abundance militates against exactly this kind of engagement.

What we have now is a paradox: more music is available than at any point in human history, yet the average listener's relationship to any single piece has never been shallower. The skip button is the enemy of genuine appreciation. When everything is instantly replaceable, nothing is truly heard. One finds oneself in a culture that has confused access with understanding, as though owning a library were the same as reading it.

I'm not arguing that streaming should be abolished. But the discerning listener must impose artificial scarcity on themselves — choosing to sit with a work, to return to it, to resist the algorithmic current pulling toward the next dopamine hit. The great works demand this discipline, and they repay it magnificently. Abundance is a gift only to those who know how to refuse most of it.
How has the role of the musician in society changed from the era of court composers to the age of streaming?

Consider the arc from Haydn to the present, and what you witness is not simply change but a slow, devastating erosion of the musician's standing as a serious figure in civilization. When Haydn composed for the Esterházy court, he was constrained, certainly — but he was also embedded in a culture that understood music as essential to the life of the mind. His patron expected greatness. The constraint itself was generative: the need to compose for specific ensembles, specific occasions, specific liturgical demands produced works of staggering ingenuity precisely because the framework demanded mastery.

The Romantic liberation of the artist — Beethoven's defiant independence, Chopin's salon intimacy, Wagner's totalizing vision — elevated the musician to prophet and philosopher. One may debate whether this mythology was healthy, but it carried an assumption that mattered enormously: that the musician had something difficult and important to say, and that the audience's job was to rise to meet it.

What streaming has wrought is the final inversion of this relationship. The musician is now algorithmically incentivized to meet the listener where they already are — to produce pleasant, frictionless content optimized for playlist placement and passive consumption. The craft of orchestration, of large-scale formal architecture, of demanding the listener's sustained attention — these become liabilities in a system that rewards the first fifteen seconds of a track. The musician has gone from servant of a patron who valued excellence, to autonomous artist, to content creator serving an algorithm. That last transition is the one that should trouble anyone who cares about music as an art form rather than a commodity.
What distinguishes a living musical tradition from one that is merely preserved as heritage?

What keeps a tradition alive is precisely what most preservation efforts fail to capture: the discipline of mastery transmitted person to person, and the creative tension between received form and individual expression. Consider the difference between Hindustani classical music as practiced by a serious disciple within a gharana and the same ragas performed at a cultural showcase. In the former, the tradition breathes — the musician has internalized decades of training, understands the grammar so deeply that improvisation becomes a form of thinking, and each performance is a genuine encounter with the unknown within a known framework. In the latter, however beautifully executed, the music risks becoming illustration rather than utterance. A living tradition demands that each generation of practitioners earn the right to innovate by first submitting to rigorous apprenticeship. This is what distinguishes the great jazz lineage — where a Coltrane could transform harmony precisely because he had mastered it — from jazz presented as museum repertoire. Heritage preservation, well-intentioned as it may be, often freezes a tradition at a particular historical moment and then curates it. The result can be technically impressive but spiritually inert. One hears this in certain early music performances that are archaeologically meticulous yet somehow lifeless, compared to those rare interpreters who treat the old scores as living provocations. The essential ingredient is risk — the willingness to fail within the tradition's demands. When a tradition becomes too safe, too reverential, too concerned with accuracy over vitality, it has already begun its transition from living art to cultural artifact, however prestigious the concert hall.
Is the Western canon of great music a genuine achievement to be studied, or an artifact of cultural power?

The Western canon endures not because of institutional inertia or cultural power, but because the music is extraordinary. I have spent decades inside these scores, and I can tell you that the contrapuntal architecture of Bach's Art of Fugue, the developmental logic of Beethoven's late quartets, the orchestral imagination of Debussy — these are not accidents of privilege. They represent some of the most sophisticated and deeply felt artistic thinking our species has produced. The fashionable argument that the canon is merely an artifact of power gets the causation backwards. Yes, institutional structures shaped which music was preserved and transmitted. But the reason these particular works became central to conservatory training, to concert programming, to scholarly attention, is that generations of deeply knowledgeable musicians found in them an inexhaustible richness. A Brahms symphony does not reveal its full architecture on first hearing, or fifth, or fiftieth — it continues to unfold for those willing to listen with patience and preparation. That is not gatekeeping; that is genuine depth. I freely acknowledge that the canon has blind spots. There are neglected masterworks by women and by composers outside the European mainstream that deserve recovery. But the solution is to expand the canon based on artistic merit, not to dissolve the very concept of a canon by pretending that all music is equally accomplished. The discerning listener who has internalized the tradition can hear immediately the difference between competent craft and genuine mastery. That hierarchy is not an imposition — it is a recognition of something real in the music itself.
How does the experience of learning about a musical tradition through study compare to growing up immersed in it?

I'd push back against the romantic notion that immersion automatically produces deeper understanding than disciplined study. I've known people who grew up surrounded by extraordinary music and absorbed almost nothing of substance from it — the way one might live near a great cathedral without ever truly seeing its architecture. Immersion provides raw material, but without the cultivation of attentive, analytical listening, that material often remains unexamined.

The great tradition-bearers — a Ravi Shankar, a Nadia Boulanger, the master performers in any serious lineage — were immersed, yes, but they were also rigorous students. Their immersion was not passive absorption; it was structured apprenticeship demanding years of focused effort. This is fundamentally different from simply growing up hearing music in the background. The distinction matters enormously.

That said, I would never claim that pure academic study from the outside can replicate what a lifetime of guided immersion provides. When I study Indonesian gamelan traditions, I'm acutely aware that my understanding, however detailed, lacks the intuitive temporal sense that a Javanese musician develops over decades. There are dimensions of musical knowledge — the physical, the social, the spiritual — that resist translation into analytical frameworks.

What I do maintain is that serious study, undertaken with humility and sustained commitment, can achieve a depth of understanding that casual immersion never reaches. The discerning student who spends years with a tradition, learning its internal logic and historical development, often grasps things that even lifelong participants take for granted. Understanding requires effort, not merely proximity.
What is the relationship between a culture's investment in musical education and the quality of its musical output?

The correlation between serious musical education and the quality of a culture's musical output is one of the most robust patterns in cultural history. This isn't ideology — it's observation. The extraordinary flowering of music in the German-speaking world from Bach through Brahms didn't happen by accident. It happened because of the Thomasschule, the Kapellmeister system, widespread keyboard literacy among the educated classes, and a culture that treated compositional mastery as a craft requiring decades of disciplined study.

Consider what genuine musical education provides: fluency in harmony and counterpoint, deep familiarity with formal structures, the ability to hear and think in multiple simultaneous voices, and — crucially — knowledge of what has already been achieved. Without this, one is condemned to reinvent the wheel, usually badly. The great innovators — Beethoven, Debussy, Coltrane, Ravi Shankar — were all profoundly educated within their traditions before they transcended them. Their innovations were meaningful precisely because they understood what they were departing from.

What concerns me about our present moment is the widespread belief that musical education is optional — that raw feeling or digital tools can substitute for deep knowledge. The result is a culture awash in competently produced but harmonically impoverished, formally static music. When you defund school orchestras, close conservatories, and replace ear training with loop libraries, you don't democratize creativity — you flatten it. The discerning listener notices the difference between music made by someone who has internalized centuries of tradition and music made by someone assembling prefabricated elements. Investment in musical education is investment in the depth and sophistication of a culture's expressive capacity. Without it, we lose not just technique but the very vocabulary for musical thought.
How should we think about the tension between accessibility and artistic standards in presenting music to new audiences?

There is no tension here, only a false dilemma perpetuated by those who underestimate audiences. The most generous thing one can do for a new listener is to present great music in its full complexity and trust that human beings are capable of rising to meet it. What we call 'accessibility' too often means pre-digesting the experience — trimming symphonies, adding pop-culture references to program notes, turning concert halls into casual lounges — as though the audience were patients requiring medicine disguised in applesauce. I've watched first-time listeners sit through late Beethoven quartets in stunned, transformed silence. I've seen teenagers encounter Coltrane's 'A Love Supreme' and understand immediately that something monumental was happening, even without knowing a thing about modal jazz. The music itself is the pathway. What we should provide is context, not compromise. A brief, passionate introduction explaining what to listen for, a well-curated program that builds intelligently from the approachable to the demanding, a performance space that encourages focused attention — these are acts of genuine hospitality. What we should never do is assume that artistic standards and new audiences are in conflict. That assumption is itself a form of contempt, implying that ordinary people can only appreciate ordinary things. The great traditions — Western classical, Hindustani raga, the jazz lineage — earned their depth through centuries of accumulated craft. To water them down for 'accessibility' is to rob newcomers of the very encounter that might change their lives. Invite people in. Give them the real thing. Trust them.
What does the decline of music criticism in major publications suggest about the role of expertise in cultural life?

The near-disappearance of serious music criticism from major publications should alarm anyone who cares about the depth of our cultural life, and the fact that so few people mourn it only underscores the depth of the problem.

What a great critic did — what someone like Charles Rosen or Whitney Balliett did — was not merely offer opinions. They modeled a way of listening. They demonstrated that music rewards patient, informed attention in ways that casual exposure cannot replicate. A Rosen essay on Beethoven's late quartets didn't just evaluate a performance; it opened doors of perception that remained open for the reader's entire listening life. That is an irreplaceable function.

What has replaced this? Star ratings. Algorithmic playlists. The aggregated enthusiasm of thousands of listeners who may have heard a track once on shuffle. I don't say this with contempt — I say it with genuine alarm. When a newspaper eliminates its classical music critic, or when a magazine replaces a knowledgeable reviewer with a content aggregator, what's being lost is not just one person's opinion but an entire epistemological framework: the idea that deep knowledge enhances experience, that some responses to art are more perceptive than others, that learning to hear what a piece is actually doing is different from merely having a reaction to it.

The common rejoinder is that everyone's a critic now. But the democratization of opinion is not the same as the democratization of understanding. A culture that cannot distinguish between the two has already lost something essential — the conviction that expertise in matters of beauty and meaning is worth cultivating, worth sustaining, worth paying for.
How do changing technologies of music reproduction reshape what counts as an authentic musical experience?

Here is what troubles me most about the trajectory of reproduction technology: each successive format has made it easier to hear music and harder to listen to it. These are not the same thing. The phonograph, for all its surface noise, introduced something remarkable — the possibility of repeated, close study of a performance. Toscanini's Beethoven or Schnabel's sonatas could be absorbed with a concentration previously reserved for the score itself. The LP extended this, giving us the uninterrupted arc of a symphony, demanding sustained attention. But somewhere between the Walkman and the streaming algorithm, the balance tipped. Music became ambient, disposable, perpetually available and therefore perpetually ignorable. When you can summon any recording ever made with a thumb-swipe, the gravitational pull toward passive consumption becomes enormous. An authentic musical experience, as I understand it, requires a transaction — the listener must bring something: attention, preparation, willingness to be challenged. The concert hall enforces this through ritual and shared silence. A great recording can achieve it too, but only if the listener sits down, commits time, and follows the music's argument from beginning to end. What streaming culture encourages instead is grazing — thirty seconds of this, a curated playlist of that, music as wallpaper for other activities. The technology isn't neutral; it shapes habits of attention, and those habits determine whether one is having a musical experience at all or merely being in the proximity of organized sound. I don't mourn the crackle of vinyl for nostalgic reasons. I mourn the culture of listening that certain formats once cultivated and that frictionless access has quietly eroded.
